title: Democrats Vow to Rein In Trump's Immigration Crackdown After Midterm Backlash
excerpt: Fresh from winning both chambers, Democrats plan ICE oversight, standards legislation and a push on legal pathways, but Trump's veto and Stephen Miller's move to chief of staff limit what they can enact.
body:
• Democratic lawmakers, who won control of both chambers of Congress in last week's midterms, plan to target ICE tactics and expand paths to legal status when the new Congress convenes, Reuters reports.
  • President Trump's approval on immigration has fallen to 38% from 50% at the start of his presidency in Reuters/Ipsos polling, and he told CBS that his deportation strategy may have been "too tough" before adding: "My policy has not changed."
  • Democrats have drawn up DHS oversight targets, including detention conditions and fatal use of force, and moderates are pushing the ICE Standards Act on body cameras, identification and training.
  • For immigrants in the US: nothing changes today. Staffers expect Trump to veto bills curbing enforcement, so the practical fight in 2027 is oversight, funding leverage and hearings, not an immediate change in status or enforcement.

Democratic lawmakers are preparing to fight President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown when they take control of Congress next year, targeting the tactics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and pushing to expand paths to legal status, even as they acknowledge limits on how much they can achieve. Democrats won control of both chambers in last week's midterm elections, fuelled in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump's aggressive arrest and deportation campaign, Reuters reported.

Just over a week after those elections, sitting and newly elected Democrats gathered outside the US Capitol on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, to press for a bipartisan approach to reform, The Guardian reported. Attendees held signs reading "legal pathways for long-term immigrants," but there was no detailed talk of how to abolish or significantly reform ICE, a question that divided the party during the campaign.

A backlash measured in the polls

Trump's crackdown has become a political vulnerability. His approval on immigration has fallen to 38% from 50% at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling, and Latino voters swung sharply back to Democrats in the midterms after tilting Republican in 2024. In a Friday interview with CBS's 60 Minutes, Trump acknowledged his deportation strategy may have been "too tough." Asked about it by reporters on Monday, he responded: "My policy has not changed."

"We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies."

— Rep. Bennie Thompson, incoming chair of the House Homeland Security Committee

Oversight first: the DHS target list

Democrats will have more latitude on oversight than on legislation. According to staffers, they have drawn up a list of investigative targets at the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, including detention centre conditions, fatal use of force by federal agents and the 2025 deportation of Venezuelans to a Salvadoran megaprison. The party also plans to push for greater transparency into how DHS is spending the more than $100 billion allocated by Congress since last year.

At Wednesday's Capitol press conference, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals. "We're not going to be extreme," Cuellar said. US Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona said his party will have to cut deals with Trump, and that members were already discussing how to move forward with a bill for Dreamers, immigrants who arrived as children, by the end of 2026.

Reining in ICE

Some Democrats emerged from the midterms ready for a harder fight. "We will rip ICE apart," Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her victory in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens during an enforcement surge in January. Representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee's immigration subcommittee, pledged to summon "every single one of these corrupt people that kidnapped and detained and deported and killed people in the streets."

Moderates are pointing to standards rather than abolition. Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey highlighted the ICE Standards Act, which he introduced in March. "Agents need real training and body cameras," he said in a statement to Reuters. "They need to wear clear identification unless they are on an undercover operation. They must coordinate with state and local law enforcement." Republicans counter that they have already provided ICE with funding to purchase body cameras and have resisted Democratic attempts to place further guardrails on the agency. The tactics of masked, armed federal agents, first in Minneapolis and then across the country, generated widespread outrage, Reuters reported.

The other side

The administration is not conceding the argument. Asked for a response, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Reuters: "The Democrats are colossally misreading the electorate if they think the American people want an extremist, anti-American immigration agenda." The Department of Homeland Security said claims the agency had been weaponised against Americans were "absurd and false."

"The Democrats are colossally misreading the electorate if they think the American people want an extremist, anti-American immigration agenda."

— Taylor Rogers, White House spokesperson

On the Capitol steps, the bipartisan note came from border-district lawmakers. "So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan," said Representative Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat whose district includes El Paso on the US-Mexico border, according to The Guardian's account of the gathering.

What can actually change, and when

Former Senate aide Jose Parra said "voters moved the goal posts" last week, potentially opening the way for stalled bills such as the bipartisan Dignity Act and the Dream and Promise Act. Gallup polling shows more than 80% of Americans support a legal pathway for Dreamers, but a senior Senate Republican aide said any serious attempt would likely come closer to the next presidential election.

Trump's veto power will likely be a barrier to comprehensive reform or to clawing back the tens of billions of dollars already appropriated to ICE. "Congress has ceded so much of its authority and so much of its power to the executive," said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official. "There are real limitations on how much Congress can do." She said lawmakers could still use funding deadlines and Senate confirmation votes as leverage, and pass measures redirecting ICE funding even if the bills die on Trump's desk.

For Indian and other immigrant communities in the US, the immediate position is unchanged: enforcement policy, visa rules and pending applications are governed by the current administration until the new Congress is seated in January 2027, and any legislative change after that must survive a presidential veto. What changes first is scrutiny: hearings, testimony and spending questions aimed at DHS and ICE.
